claim: hIAPP fibrils are associated with Type-II Diabetes.
source: hIAPP fibrils are associated with Type-II Diabetes, but the link of hIAPP structure to islet cell death remains elusive.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known association in the field.

claim: hIAPP fibrils are cytotoxic to cultured pancreatic β-cells.
source: Here we observe that hIAPP fibrils are cytotoxic to cultured pancreatic β-cells, leading us to determine the structure and cytotoxicity of protein segments composing the amyloid spine of hIAPP.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations described in the abstract and detailed in Figure 1.

claim: Segment 19–29 S20G forms pairs of β-sheets mated by a dry interface.
source: Using the cryoEM method MicroED, we discover that one segment, 19–29 S20G, forms pairs of β-sheets mated by a dry interface that share structural features with and are similarly cytotoxic to full-length hIAPP fibrils.
evidence: This structural determination is based on MicroED data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Segment 19–29 S20G is cytotoxic.
source: Using the cryoEM method MicroED, we discover that one segment, 19–29 S20G, forms pairs of β-sheets mated by a dry interface that share structural features with and are similarly cytotoxic to full-length hIAPP fibrils.
evidence: Cytotoxicity is demonstrated through MTT reduction and caspase activation assays shown in Figure 5.

claim: Segment 15–25 WT forms non-toxic labile β-sheets.
source: In contrast, a second segment, 15–25 WT, forms non-toxic labile β-sheets.
evidence: This is supported by structural data from MicroED and cytotoxicity assays showing no toxicity.

claim: Both segments 19–29 S20G and 15–25 WT can seed full-length hIAPP.
source: These segments possess different structures and cytotoxic effects, however, both can seed full-length hIAPP, and cause hIAPP to take on the cytotoxic and structural features of that segment.
evidence: Seeding experiments are shown in Figure 1G and Figure 6.

claim: Seeding with different segments causes hIAPP to adopt the cytotoxic and structural features of that segment.
source: These segments possess different structures and cytotoxic effects, however, both can seed full-length hIAPP, and cause hIAPP to take on the cytotoxic and structural features of that segment.
evidence: This is demonstrated by seeding experiments showing different cytotoxicity profiles in Figure 6.

claim: Segment 19–29 S20G may serve as a model for the toxic spine of hIAPP.
source: These results suggest that protein segment structures represent polymorphs of their parent protein and that segment 19–29 S20G may serve as a model for the toxic spine of hIAPP.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural and functional similarities between the segment and full-length hIAPP.

claim: Amyloid fibrils are associated with more than 25 diseases.
source: Amyloid fibrils are associated with more than 25 diseases, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and Type-II Diabetes (T2D) (Eisenberg and Jucker, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Eisenberg and Jucker, 2012.

claim: In Type-II Diabetes, amyloid fibrils are composed of human islet amyloid polypeptide (hIAPP).
source: The fibrils observed in each disease are composed of a particular protein; in T2D, amyloid fibrils are composed of human islet amyloid polypeptide (hIAPP) (Westermark et al., 1987; Cooper et al., 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Westermark et al., 1987 and Cooper et al., 1988.

claim: hIAPP is a 37 residue polypeptide hormone that is co-secreted with insulin to modulate glucose levels.
source: hIAPP is a 37 residue polypeptide hormone that is co-secreted with insulin to modulate glucose levels (Roberts et al., 1989; Westermark et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Roberts et al., 1989 and Westermark et al., 2011.

claim: Approximately 90% of pancreatic tissue samples taken post-mortem from T2D patients contain islet amyloid primarily composed of hIAPP.
source: Approximately 90% of pancreatic tissue samples taken post-mortem from T2D patients contain islet amyloid primarily composed of hIAPP (Höppener et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Höppener et al., 2000.

claim: The extent of islet amyloid positively correlates with pancreatic β-cell loss and insulin dependence.
source: The extent of islet amyloid positively correlates with pancreatic β-cell loss and insulin dependence (Maloy et al., 1981; Esapa et al., 2005; Jurgens et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Maloy et al., 1981; Esapa et al., 2005; Jurgens et al., 2011.

claim: Mouse IAPP differs from human IAPP by only six residues, 3 of which are β-strand breaking prolines.
source: mouse IAPP differs from human IAPP by only six residues, 3 of which are β-strand breaking prolines.
evidence: This is a known sequence comparison between mouse and human IAPP.

claim: Mouse IAPP does not aggregate.
source: Consequently, mouse IAPP does not aggregate (Nishi et al., 1989; Westermark et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nishi et al., 1989 and Westermark et al., 1990.

claim: Mice can be induced to develop islet amyloid and T2D when they are engineered to express human IAPP and fed a high fat diet.
source: Moreover, mice can be induced to develop islet amyloid and T2D when they are engineered to express human IAPP and fed a high fat diet (Verchere et al., 1996; Westermark et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Verchere et al., 1996 and Westermark et al., 2000.

claim: The hIAPP-S20G mutation is associated with early onset T2D in families who carry this lesion.
source: Perhaps the strongest support for a link is the mutation in hIAPP, hIAPP-S20G; segments that contain this mutation aggregate more quickly, contribute to increased pancreatic β-cell apoptosis, and are associated with early onset T2D in families who carry this lesion (Sakagashira et al., 2000; Cao et al., 2012; Meier et al., 2016; Sakagashira et al., 1996; Lee et al., 2001; Morita et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations including Sakagashira et al., 2000; Cao et al., 2012; Meier et al., 2016.

claim: Segments containing the S20G mutation aggregate more quickly.
source: Perhaps the strongest support for a link is the mutation in hIAPP, hIAPP-S20G; segments that contain this mutation aggregate more quickly, contribute to increased pancreatic β-cell apoptosis, and are associated with early onset T2D in families who carry this lesion (Sakagashira et al., 2000; Cao et al., 2012; Meier et al., 2016; Sakagashira et al., 1996; Lee et al., 2001; Morita et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on the S20G mutation.

claim: Segments containing the S20G mutation contribute to increased pancreatic β-cell apoptosis.
source: Perhaps the strongest support for a link is the mutation in hIAPP, hIAPP-S20G; segments that contain this mutation aggregate more quickly, contribute to increased pancreatic β-cell apoptosis, and are associated with early onset T2D in families who carry this lesion (Sakagashira et al., 2000; Cao et al., 2012; Meier et al., 2016; Sakagashira et al., 1996; Lee et al., 2001; Morita et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on the S20G mutation.

claim: hIAPP aged for 24 h contains amyloid fibrils and no detectable oligomers.
source: (A) Human IAPP (hIAPP) aged for 24 h contains amyloid fibrils and no detectable oligomers.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ThT binding, TEM, and dot blot assays shown in Figure 1A.

claim: hIAPP aged for 24 h is significantly more cytotoxic than hIAPP aged for 0 h.
source: (B) and (C) hIAPP aged for 24 h is significantly more cytotoxic than hIAPP aged for 0 h.
evidence: This is demonstrated by MTT reduction and caspase-3/7 activation assays shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: Mouse IAPP does not form amyloid fibrils.
source: Mouse IAPP (mIAPP), which does not form amyloid fibrils, is not cytotoxic regardless of time period of aging.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: Mouse IAPP is not cytotoxic regardless of time period of aging.
source: Mouse IAPP (mIAPP), which does not form amyloid fibrils, is not cytotoxic regardless of time period of aging.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: Rin5F cells treated with hIAPP aged for 24 h reduce significantly less MTT dye than Rin5F cells treated with hIAPP aged for 0 h.
source: (B) Rin5F cells treated with hIAPP aged for 24 h reduce significantly less MTT dye than Rin5F cells treated with hIAPP aged for 0 h (ns=not significant; ****p<0.0001 using an unpaired t-test with equal standard deviations).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MTT reduction assay data shown in Figure 1B with statistical analysis.

claim: Rin5F cells treated with hIAPP aged for 24 h exhibit significantly higher caspase-3/7 activation than Rin5F cells treated with hIAPP aged for 0 h.
source: (C) Rin5F cells treated with hIAPP aged for 24 h exhibit significantly higher caspase-3/7 activation than Rin5F cells treated with hIAPP aged for 0 h.
evidence: This is demonstrated by caspase-3/7 activation assay data shown in Figure 1C with statistical analysis.

claim: The insoluble fraction of hIAPP aged 24 h contains the cytotoxic species.
source: (D) The insoluble fraction of hIAPP aged 24 h, which contains amyloid fibrils and no detectable oligomers, contains the cytotoxic species.
evidence: This is demonstrated by cytotoxicity assays on fractionated samples shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Fibrils of spine segments seed hIAPP fibril formation.
source: (G) Fibrils of spine segments seed hIAPP fibril formation, suggesting that spine segments embody structural characteristics of full-length hIAPP fibrils.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ThT fluorescence assays shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Mouse IAPP does not seed hIAPP fibril formation.
source: mIAPP, which does not contain amyloid fibrils, does not seed hIAPP fibril formation.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1G.

claim: 3D crystals of 19–29 S20G diffract to 1.6 Å using MicroED.
source: (A) 3D crystals of 19–29 S20G (right, inset) diffract to 1.6 Å using MicroED, a whole angstrom better resolution than the microcrystals of 19–29 S20G (left, inset).
evidence: This is demonstrated by diffraction patterns shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 3D crystals of 15–25 WT diffract to 1.4 Å using MicroED.
source: (B) 3D crystals of 15–25 WT (right, inset) diffract to 1.4 Å using MicroED, whereas microcrystals of 15–25 WT diffract to 2.2 Å using Microfocus X-rays (left, inset).
evidence: This is demonstrated by diffraction patterns shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The dry interface of 19–29 S20G buries 265 Å2 of surface area per strand.
source: The dry interface buries 265 Å2 of surface area per strand, which equates to 24 Å2 per residue.
evidence: This is calculated from the atomic structure determined by MicroED.

claim: The dry interface of 19–29 S20G has a shape complementarity of 0.85.
source: This interface is one of the largest and most complementary of any structurally determined steric-zipper interface (Supplementary file 1); it has a shape complementary of 0.85.
evidence: This is calculated from the atomic structure.

claim: The fiber diffraction pattern calculated from the 19–29 S20G structure shares key features with fiber diffraction collected from full-length hIAPP fibrils.
source: The similarity between the fiber diffraction pattern calculated from this steric-zipper and the fiber diffraction pattern collected from full-length hIAPP fibrils tends to validate the 19–29 S20G atomic structure as a model for the amyloid spine of full-length hIAPP (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison of calculated and experimental fiber diffraction patterns in Figure 3D.

claim: The diffraction patterns of 19–29 S20G and full-length hIAPP share a reflection at 3.7 Å along the off-meridian.
source: Additionally, along the off-meridonal, the diffraction patterns share a reflection at 3.7 Å.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The diffraction patterns of 19–29 S20G and full-length hIAPP share reflections at 10.0 Å and 5.0 Å along the equator.
source: Along the equator (right panel), the dry interface and full-length hIAPP fibrils share reflections at 10.0 Å and 5.0 Å (black arrows).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D.

claim: 15–25 WT forms an arrangement of unmated β-sheets composed of anti-parallel out-of-register β-strands.
source: The atomic structure of segment 15–25 WT, also determined using MicroED (Figure 2B; Figure 4A), shows an arrangement of unmated β-sheets composed of anti-parallel out-of-register β-strands that is uncharacteristic of pathogenic amyloid fibrils (Figure 4B;Table 1).
evidence: This is determined from the MicroED structure shown in Figure 4.

claim: 15–25 WT fibrils completely disaggregate in the presence of heat and 1% SDS.
source: Turbidity readings followed by negative-stain EM reveal that 15–25 WT fibrils completely disaggregate in the presence of heat and 1% SDS, but 19–29 S20G fibrils remain intact in up to 2% SDS (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by turbidity measurements and EM shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: 19–29 S20G fibrils remain intact in up to 2% SDS.
source: Turbidity readings followed by negative-stain EM reveal that 15–25 WT fibrils completely disaggregate in the presence of heat and 1% SDS, but 19–29 S20G fibrils remain intact in up to 2% SDS (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by turbidity measurements and EM shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: 15–25 WT and 15–25 S20G fibrils are not toxic compared to full-length hIAPP fibrils.
source: (A) 15–25 WT and 15–25 S20G fibrils are not toxic compared to full-length hIAPP fibrils (n = 12 across four biological replicates, each with three technical replicates).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MTT reduction assays shown in Figure 5A.

claim: 19–29 S20G fibrils are significantly more cytotoxic than 19–29 WT fibrils.
source: (B) 19–29 WT fibrils are mildly cytotoxic and 19–29 S20G fibrils are significantly more cytotoxic than 19–29 WT fibrils (****p<0.0001 using a Mann-Whitney U test; n = 12 across four biological replicates, each with three technical replicates).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MTT reduction assays shown in Figure 5B with statistical analysis.

claim: 19–29 S20G fibrils (10 μM) are similarly cytotoxic to full-length hIAPP fibrils at the same concentration.
source: 19–29 S20G fibrils (10 μM) are similarly cytotoxic to full-length hIAPP fibrils at the same concentration (lower dashed line) (p=0.09 using an unpaired t-test with equal standard deviations).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MTT reduction assays shown in Figure 5B with statistical analysis.

claim: The insoluble fraction of the 19–29 S20G cytotoxic preparation contains the cytotoxic species.
source: (C) The insoluble fraction of the 50 μM 19–29 S20G cytotoxic preparation contains the cytotoxic species.
evidence: This is demonstrated by MTT reduction assays on fractionated samples shown in Figure 5C.

claim: 19–29 S20G fibrils induce the most caspase-3 activity among the spine segments.
source: Using a FRET-based biosensor assay for monitoring caspase-3 activity in real-time, 19–29 S20G fibrils induce the most caspase-3 activity, whereas segments 15–25 did not induce caspase-3 activity, consistent with the MTT dye reduction assay results.
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRET-based caspase-3 assays shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: Segments 15–25 did not induce caspase-3 activity.
source: Using a FRET-based biosensor assay for monitoring caspase-3 activity in real-time, 19–29 S20G fibrils induce the most caspase-3 activity, whereas segments 15–25 did not induce caspase-3 activity, consistent with the MTT dye reduction assay results.
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRET-based caspase-3 assays shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: EGCG mitigates 19–29 S20G fibril formation.
source: (B) Negative-stain electron micrographs reveal that EGCG mitigates 19–29 S20G fibril formation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by negative-stain EM shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: EGCG mitigates 19–29 S20G cytotoxicity.
source: (C) EGCG mitigates 19–29 S20G cytotoxicity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by MTT reduction assays shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claim: EGCG does not mitigate fibril formation of 15–25 WT.
source: (D) Negative-stain EM reveals that EGCG does not mitigate fibril formation of 15–25 WT, a spine segment that does not possess a hydrophobic core.
evidence: This is demonstrated by negative-stain EM shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D.

claim: hIAPP seeded with stable, toxic 19–29 S20G fibrils is more cytotoxic to Rin5F cells than hIAPP seeded with labile, non-toxic 15–25 WT fibrils.
source: hIAPP seeded with stable, toxic 19–29 S20G fibrils is more cytotoxic to Rin5F cells than hIAPP seeded with labile, non-toxic 15–25 WT fibrils.
evidence: This is demonstrated by MTT reduction assays shown in Figure 6 with statistical analysis.

claim: 19–29 S20G seeds and 15–25 WT seeds (100 nM each) are not cytotoxic to Rin5F cells.
source: 19–29 S20G seeds and 15–25 WT seeds (100 nM each) are not cytotoxic to Rin5F cells.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6.

claim: hIAPP fibrils formed by seeding with stable, toxic 19–29 S20G fibrils exhibit shorter equatorial Bragg spacings than hIAPP seeded with labile, non-toxic 15–25 WT fibrils.
source: hIAPP fibrils formed by seeding with stable, toxic 19–29 S20G fibrils exhibit reflections indicative of shorter equatorial Bragg spacings than hIAPP seeded with labile, non-toxic 15–25 WT fibrils (9.0 Å versus 10.0 Å) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by X-ray fiber diffraction and radial profile analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Dr. Eugene Opie first observed islet amyloid in post-mortem pancreata of T2D patients in 1901.
source: In 1901, when Dr. Eugene Opie first observed islet amyloid in post-mortem pancreata of T2D patients, he proposed a link between the islet amyloid and T2D (Opie, 1901).
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by citation to Opie, 1901.

claim: The 19–29 S20G atomic structure recapitulates many of the structural features and cytotoxic properties of hIAPP.
source: The experiments of this study show that the 19–29 S20G atomic structure recapitulates many of the structural features and cytotoxic properties of hIAPP.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Preparations of 19–29 S20G that contain fibrils are cytotoxic, as is the case for full-length hIAPP.
source: First, preparations of 19–29 S20G that contain fibrils are cytotoxic, as is the case for full-length hIAPP.
evidence: This is demonstrated by cytotoxicity assays shown in Figures 1 and 5.

claim: Segment 19–29 S20G elicits cytotoxicity by altering cell metabolism and activating pro-apoptotic machinery.
source: Third, segment 19–29 S20G elicits cytotoxicity by altering cell metabolism and activating pro-apoptotic machinery, mechanisms by which full-length hIAPP fibrils are thought to contribute to pancreatic β-cell death during T2D.
evidence: This is demonstrated by MTT reduction and caspase activation assays shown in Figure 5.

claim: The early onset S20G mutation confers greater cytotoxicity within segment 19–29 and within full-length hIAPP.
source: Fourth, the early onset S20G mutation confers greater cytotoxicity within segment 19–29 and within full-length hIAPP.
evidence: This is demonstrated by cytotoxicity assays comparing WT and S20G variants.

claim: EGCG mitigates full-length hIAPP fibril formation and cytotoxicity.
source: Last, EGCG, a flavanol that mitigates full-length hIAPP fibril formation and cytotoxicity, likewise mitigates 19–29 S20G fibril formation and cytotoxicity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Segment 19–29 S20G represents the toxic amyloid spine of hIAPP.
source: These results, taken together with the canonical pathogenic amyloid fibril architecture of segment 19–29 S20G, suggest it represents the toxic amyloid spine of hIAPP.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural and functional data presented.

claim: Not all hIAPP fibril structures are cytotoxic.
source: Additionally, our studies suggest that not all hIAPP fibril structures are cytotoxic.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that 15–25 WT forms fibrils but is not cytotoxic.

claim: The curved β-sheets in the 19–29 S20G structure accommodate the tightly packed hydrophobic core while maintaining high shape complementarity and large buried surface area.
source: In the dry interface of the 19–29 S20G atomic structure, the curved β-sheets accommodate the tightly packed hydrophobic core, which includes a bulky phenylalanine, while maintaining high shape complementarity and large buried surface area.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural features observed in the atomic structure.

claim: In the 15–25 WT structure, the curved β-sheets prevent adjacent sheets from associating to form a canonical pathogenic amyloid fibril architecture.
source: Paradoxically, in the 15–25 WT atomic structure, the curved β-sheets appear to have an opposite effect: the curved β-sheets appear to prevent adjacent sheets from associating to form a canonical pathogenic amyloid fibril architecture.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural features observed in the atomic structure.

claim: The out-of-register protein segment KDWSFY from β2-microglobulin elicits mild cytotoxicity.
source: Here, we show that 15–25 WT is not cytotoxic but in contrast, the out-of-register protein segment KDWSFY from β2-microglobulin elicits mild cytotoxicity (Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2012.

claim: The KDWSFY structure is formed of sheets mated by a dry interface.
source: One notable difference between the two structures is that the 15–25 WT structure is formed of single sheets, while the KDWSFY structure is formed of sheets mated by a dry interface.
evidence: This is a comparison of structural features from different protein segment structures.

claim: The dry interface of the KDWSFY atomic structure results in a higher solvation energy per strand compared to the 15–25 WT atomic structure (122 cal/mol/strand vs. 19 cal/mol/strand).
source: The dry interface of the KDWSFY atomic structure results in a higher solvation energy per strand compared to the 15–25 WT atomic structure (122 cal/mol/strand vs. 19 cal/mol/strand).
evidence: This is calculated from the atomic structures.

claim: Cytotoxic structures like 19–29 S20G have relatively high solvation energies per strand (279 cal/mol/strand).
source: Given that cytotoxic structures like 19–29 S20G have relatively high solvation energies per strand (279 cal/mol/strand; Supplementary file 1), this difference may explain the disparate cytotoxic effects of the two out-of-register structures.
evidence: This is calculated from the atomic structure and presented in Supplementary file 1.

claim: The nature of cytotoxicity is not simply conferred by in-register or out-of-register structures.
source: The disparate cytotoxic effects within this structure class lead us to believe that the nature of cytotoxicity is not simply conferred by in-register or out-of-register structures.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing cytotoxicity of different structural classes.

claim: 19–29 WT fibrils are likely polymorphic and may contain some fraction of fibrils that are structurally similar to non-toxic 15–25 WT fibrils.
source: Although the 19–29 WT fibrils prepared in this study appear morphologically similar to 19–29 S20G fibrils, the 19–29 WT fibrils are likely polymorphic and may contain some fraction of fibrils that are structurally similar to non-toxic 15–25 WT fibrils.
evidence: This is a speculation based on previous structural studies and the observed lower cytotoxicity of 19–29 WT.

claim: Previous structural studies of segment 20–29 WT fibrils show that it forms an array of polymorphs, some of which are similar to the 15–25 WT atomic structure.
source: Previous structural studies of segment 20–29 WT fibrils show that it forms an array of polymorphs, some of which are similar to the 15–25 WT atomic structure (Griffiths et al., 1995; Jack et al., 2006; Madine et al., 2008; Ashburn et al., 1992; Nielsen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous structural studies.

claim: Structural polymorphism of 19–29 WT fibrils may explain their lower cytotoxicity than 19–29 S20G fibrils.
source: Structural polymorphism of 19–29 WT fibrils may explain their lower cytotoxicity than 19–29 S20G fibrils, which are homogenous in structure.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed structural and cytotoxicity differences.

claim: Raising antibodies against hIAPP fibrils may represent a promising strategy for therapeutic development.
source: In addition, if hIAPP fibrils truly are a major type of toxic aggregate that contributes to T2D, then raising antibodies against hIAPP fibrils may represent a promising strategy for therapeutic development, especially in light of the recent success of preliminary studies with antibodies raised against amyloid-β (Sevigny et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculation about potential therapeutic strategies, supported by a citation to Sevigny et al., 2016.

claim: MicroED employs a standard cryo electron microscope in diffraction mode for data collection from 3D crystals only a few hundred nanometers thick.
source: MicroED employs a standard cryo electron microscope (cryoEM) in diffraction mode for data collection from 3D crystals only a few hundred nanometers thick (Figure 2A; Figure 3A) (Shi et al., 2013; Nannenga et al., 2014a, 2014b; Hattne et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a description of the MicroED method supported by multiple citations.

claim: Nano-sized 3D crystals used for MicroED produced higher resolution diffraction than relatively larger crystals suited for structure determination at a microfocus X-ray beamline.
source: Indeed, we found that the nano-sized 3D crystals used for MicroED produced higher resolution diffraction than relatively larger crystals suited for structure determination at a microfocus X-ray beamline (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison of diffraction patterns shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Residues 15–29 compose the amyloid spine of hIAPP.
source: We identified residues 15–29 as the amyloid spine based on several lines of evidence and previous work by others (Westermark et al., 1990; Moriarty and Raleigh, 1999; Goldsbury et al., 2000; Tenidis et al., 2000).
evidence: This identification is based on multiple lines of evidence and previous work cited.

claim: The sequence of mouse IAPP differs from human IAPP only within residues 15–29.
source: First, the sequence of mouse IAPP (mIAPP), which is non-amyloidogenic, differs from human IAPP only within this region (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is shown in the sequence alignment in Figure 1E.

claim: The only known familial disease mutation in hIAPP, hIAPP-S20G, occurs within residues 15–29.
source: Second, the only known familial disease mutation in hIAPP, hIAPP-S20G, also occurs within this region (Figure 1E) (Sakagashira et al., 2000; Cao et al., 2012).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1E and supported by citations.

claim: Phe15 may be part of the amyloid spine because it is required for stabilizing an on-pathway α-helical dimer.
source: Third, previous work by our laboratory has shown that Phe15 may be part of the amyloid spine because it is required for stabilizing an on-pathway α-helical dimer and mutating this residue can delay fibril formation (Wiltzius et al., 2009b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wiltzius et al., 2009b.

claim: Mutating Phe15 can delay fibril formation.
source: Third, previous work by our laboratory has shown that Phe15 may be part of the amyloid spine because it is required for stabilizing an on-pathway α-helical dimer and mutating this residue can delay fibril formation (Wiltzius et al., 2009b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wiltzius et al., 2009b.

claim: All four spine segments form amyloid fibrils or crystals.
source: All four spine segments form amyloid fibrils or crystals (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) that seed full-length hIAPP fibril formation (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 3), suggesting that the spine segments embody structural characteristics of full-length hIAPP fibrils.
evidence: This is demonstrated by EM images in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and seeding assays in Figure 1G.

claim: Crystals that appeared visually undistorted and that were 100–300 nm thick produced the best diffraction.
source: Crystals that appeared visually undistorted and that were 100–300 nm thick produced the best diffraction.
evidence: This is an observation from the MicroED data collection process.

claim: The electron dose rate deposited onto crystals during MicroED data collection was less than 0.01 e−/Å2 per second.
source: The geometry detailed above equates to an electron dose rate of less than 0.01 e−/Å2 per second being deposited onto our crystals.
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental parameters used in MicroED data collection.

claim: The resolution of the 19–29 S20G dataset was cut off at 1.9 Å to facilitate subsequent rounds of structure refinement.
source: Of note, the resolution was cut off at 1.9 Å to facilitate subsequent rounds of structure refinement.
evidence: This is a methodological decision made during structure determination.

claim: The 19–29 S20G structure was determined using molecular replacement with an idealized 7-residue poly-alanine strand as the search model.
source: We determined the structure using molecular replacement. An idealized 7-residue poly-alanine strand led us to our atomic model.
evidence: This describes the method used for structure determination.

claim: The 15–25 WT structure was determined using molecular replacement with an out-of-register β-strand model as the search model.
source: We determined the structure using molecular replacement. Dozens of search models were used, but an out-of-register β-strand model led us to our solution.
evidence: This describes the method used for structure determination.

claim: The wet interface of 19–29 S20G buries only 153 Å2 of surface area per strand.
source: The wet interface buries only 153 Å2 of surface area per strand and it possesses a shape complementarity of 0.64.
evidence: This is calculated from the crystal structure and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The wet interface of 19–29 S20G possesses a shape complementarity of 0.64.
source: The wet interface buries only 153 Å2 of surface area per strand and it possesses a shape complementarity of 0.64.
evidence: This is calculated from the crystal structure and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The wet interface does not form the amyloid spine because the fiber diffraction pattern calculated from this interface does not match the fiber diffraction pattern collected from full-length hIAPP fibrils.
source: The wet interface does not form the amyloid spine because (1) the fiber diffraction pattern calculated from this interface does not match the fiber diffraction pattern collected from full-length hIAPP fibrils, (2) it contains waters, and (3) it possesses less side-chain interdigitation than the dry interface.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison of calculated and experimental fiber diffraction patterns in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The wet interface contains waters.
source: The wet interface does not form the amyloid spine because (1) the fiber diffraction pattern calculated from this interface does not match the fiber diffraction pattern collected from full-length hIAPP fibrils, (2) it contains waters, and (3) it possesses less side-chain interdigitation than the dry interface.
evidence: This is shown in the crystal structure in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The wet interface possesses less side-chain interdigitation than the dry interface.
source: The wet interface does not form the amyloid spine because (1) the fiber diffraction pattern calculated from this interface does not match the fiber diffraction pattern collected from full-length hIAPP fibrils, (2) it contains waters, and (3) it possesses less side-chain interdigitation than the dry interface.
evidence: This is shown in the crystal structure in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: 19–29 WT and S20G fibrils share strong reflections at 4.6 Å, 8.4–9 Å, and 34.7 Å.
source: 19–29 WT (black) and S20G (gray) fibrils share strong reflections at 4.6 Å, 8.4–9 Å, and 34.7 Å.
evidence: This is shown in the overlaid radial profiles in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claim: 15–25 WT and S20G fibrils display strong reflections at 4.7 Å, 9.3–9.8 Å, 18.2 Å, and 37.0 Å.
source: 15–25 WT (black) and S20G (gray) fibrils display strong reflections at 4.7 Å, 9.3–9.8 Å, 18.2 Å, and 37.0 Å.
evidence: This is shown in the overlaid radial profiles in Figure 4—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The early onset S20G mutation does not confer a fibril morphology distinguishable from wild-type.
source: Taken together with the X-ray fiber diffraction data from the 19–29 segments, we conclude that the early onset S20G mutation does not confer a fibril morphology distinguishable from wild-type.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the fiber diffraction data showing similar patterns for WT and S20G variants.

claim: The dry interface is formed by tightly packed, interdigitating side-chains.
source: The dry interface is formed by tightly packed, interdigitating side-chains.
evidence: This is shown in the atomic structure in Figure 3B.

claim: The dry interface excludes water molecules.
source: Pairs of β-sheets are oriented face-to-face and they are tightly mated by a dry interface that excludes water.
evidence: This is shown in the atomic structure in Figure 3B.

claim: The zipper contains a tightly packed hydrophobic core consisting of Phe23, Ala25, and Ile27.
source: This zipper contains a tightly packed hydrophobic core consisting of Phe23, Ala25, and Ile27.
evidence: This is observed in the atomic structure.

claim: Phe23 is the central and largest contributor to the hydrophobic core.
source: Phe23 is the central and largest contributor the hydrophobic core, consistent with multiple other experiments (Tenidis et al., 2000; Griffiths et al., 1995; Jack et al., 2006; Madine et al., 2008).
evidence: This is observed in the atomic structure and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The dry interface is nearly as large as the toxic core of α-synuclein.
source: The dry interface is nearly as large as the toxic core of α-synuclein (Rodriguez et al., 2015), but with higher shape complementarity.
evidence: This is a comparison with another amyloid structure supported by a citation to Rodriguez et al., 2015.

claim: The β-sheets of the 19–29 S20G atomic structure possess a curvature that is not common in shorter hIAPP protein segments.
source: The β-sheets of the 19–29 S20G atomic structure possess a curvature that is not common in shorter hIAPP protein segments (Wiltzius et al., 2008, 2009a; Soriaga et al., 2015).
evidence: This is observed by comparing RMSD values across different hIAPP segment structures.

claim: The 19–29 S20G structure ranks in the upper half of hIAPP segment structures in terms of sheet curvature.
source: The 19–29 S20G structure ranks in the upper half of the list (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), containing both sheet curvature and a sharp kink.
evidence: This is shown in the comparison of RMSD values in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The early onset Gly20 mutation adopts an unusual geometry (φ = −101.7° and ψ = 107.5°) that creates a kink in the peptide backbone.
source: The stability of the mutant segment may stem from the early onset Gly20 mutation, which adopts an unusual geometry (φ = −101.7° and ψ = 107.5°) that creates a kink in the peptide backbone.
evidence: This is observed in the atomic structure.

claim: The 19–29 S20G structure has a slightly lower energy than 19–29 WT (−590 REU vs. −535 REU).
source: The alteration separates the pair of sheets by approximately 1.5 Å in this region, and therefore the 19–29 S20G structure has a slightly lower energy than 19–29 WT (−590 REU vs. −535 REU).
evidence: This is calculated using FoldIt energy minimization.

claim: The β-strands in the 15–25 WT structure are out-of-register by two residues.
source: The β-strands are out-of-register by two residues because Leu16 on the first β-strand is directly above His18 on the third β-strand.
evidence: This is shown in the atomic structure in Figure 4B.

claim: The asymmetric unit of 15–25 WT contains density for seven ordered water molecules and one thiocyanate molecule.
source: A view down the 'proto-fibril axis' of the crystal shows that the faces of adjacent sheets are wet and overlap only partially (Figure 4C); the asymmetric unit contains density for seven ordered water molecules and one thiocyanate molecule.
evidence: This is observed in the atomic structure shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The area buried between adjacent sheets in 15–25 WT is small (10.7 Å2 per residue) compared to the average steric-zipper (20.1 Å2 per residue).
source: The area buried between adjacent sheets is small (10.7 Å2 per residue) compared to the average steric-zipper (20.1 Å2 per residue).
evidence: This is calculated from the atomic structure.

claim: hIAPP seeded with non-toxic 15–25 WT fibrils is less cytotoxic than hIAPP alone.
source: Using MTT dye reduction, we observe that hIAPP seeded with non-toxic 15–25 WT fibrils is less cytotoxic than hIAPP alone, but hIAPP seeded with stable, toxic 19–29 S20G fibrils is similarly cytotoxic to hIAPP alone (Figure 6).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MTT reduction assays shown in Figure 6.

claim: hIAPP seeded with stable, toxic 19–29 S20G fibrils is similarly cytotoxic to hIAPP alone.
source: Using MTT dye reduction, we observe that hIAPP seeded with non-toxic 15–25 WT fibrils is less cytotoxic than hIAPP alone, but hIAPP seeded with stable, toxic 19–29 S20G fibrils is similarly cytotoxic to hIAPP alone (Figure 6).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MTT reduction assays shown in Figure 6.

claim: The tighter packing of hIAPP fibrils seeded with 19–29 S20G may explain their enhanced cytotoxicity.
source: The tighter packing of these fibrils may explain their enhanced cytotoxicity.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed correlation between fibril packing and cytotoxicity.

claim: hIAPP aged for 0 h contains oligomers and no detectable amyloid fibrils.
source: (A) hIAPP aged for 0 h contains oligomers and no detectable amyloid fibrils as assessed by ThT binding, TEM, and a dot blot assay using the anti-oligomer antibody, LOC.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ThT binding, TEM, and dot blot assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The insoluble fraction of hIAPP aged for 24 h is composed of amyloid fibrils and no detectable oligomers.
source: (B) The insoluble fraction of hIAPP aged for 24 h, which contains the cytotoxic species, is composed of amyloid fibrils and no detectable oligomers.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ThT binding, TEM, and dot blot assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The soluble fraction of hIAPP aged for 24 h contains no detectable amyloid fibrils or oligomers.
source: The soluble fraction, which is not cytotoxic, contains no detectable amyloid fibrils or oligomers.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ThT binding, TEM, and dot blot assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: 15–25 WT forms striated ribbons.
source: (A) 15–25 WT forms striated ribbons.
evidence: This is shown by electron microscopy in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: 15–25 S20G forms striated ribbons.
source: (B) 15–25 S20G forms striated ribbons.
evidence: This is shown by electron microscopy in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: 19–29 WT forms both striated ribbons and twisted fibrils of varying widths.
source: (C) 19–29 WT forms both striated ribbons and twisted fibrils of varying widths.
evidence: This is shown by electron microscopy in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: 19–29 S20G forms 3D crystals only a few hundred nanometers thick.
source: (D) 19–29 S20G forms 3D crystals only a few hundred nanometers thick.
evidence: This is shown by electron microscopy in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Seeds of spine segments (1 μM) do not bind ThT.
source: (B) Seeds of spine segments (1 μM) do not bind ThT.
evidence: This is shown by ThT fluorescence measurements in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: hIAPP-WT fibrils seed hIAPP-S20G fibril formation.
source: These results are consistent with earlier findings by Cao and co-workers, who observed that hIAPP-WT fibrils seed hIAPP-S20G fibril formation, thus suggesting a shared fibrillar structure (Cao et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cao et al., 2012.

claim: A previous study of 20–29 WT fiber diffraction revealed comparable reflections to 19–29 S20G.
source: A previous study of 20–29 WT fiber diffraction revealed comparable reflections, which the authors used to formulate a fibril model of 20–29 WT that roughly agrees with our 19–29 S20G atomic structure (Madine et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Madine et al., 2008.

claim: The 19–29 S20G atomic structure and the 20–29 WT model differ by a small shift in registration between sheets.
source: Our atomic structure and their model differ by a small shift in registration between sheets, allowing for tighter packing in the atomic structure.
evidence: This is a comparison between the current structure and a previously published model.

claim: Residues 1–8 of hIAPP are required for hIAPP binding to heparan sulfate proteoglycans.
source: Segment 19–29 S20G is not as cytotoxic as full-length hIAPP in this assay, possibly because hIAPP interaction with heparan sulfate proteoglycans (HSPG) is important for apoptosis induction (Oskarsson et al., 2015), and residues 1–8, which are missing in all of the spine segments, are required for hIAPP binding to HSPG's.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Oskarsson et al., 2015.

claim: hIAPP interaction with heparan sulfate proteoglycans is important for apoptosis induction.
source: Segment 19–29 S20G is not as cytotoxic as full-length hIAPP in this assay, possibly because hIAPP interaction with heparan sulfate proteoglycans (HSPG) is important for apoptosis induction (Oskarsson et al., 2015), and residues 1–8, which are missing in all of the spine segments, are required for hIAPP binding to HSPG's.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Oskarsson et al., 2015.

claim: EGCG may mitigate hIAPP fibril formation by binding to the dry interface of the amyloid spine.
source: We hypothesize that EGCG may mitigate fibril formation of full-length hIAPP and 19–29 S20G by binding to a common site, such as the dry interface of the amyloid spine.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation that EGCG prevents fibril formation of both full-length hIAPP and 19–29 S20G.

claim: EGCG may mitigate hIAPP fibril formation by binding hIAPP via hydrophobic interactions.
source: A previous study suggested EGCG may mitigate hIAPP fibril formation by binding hIAPP via hydrophobic interactions (Young et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Young et al., 2015.
